extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, USPTO officials, patent policy makers, and patent scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reforming U.S. Patent and Trademark Office procedures and funding to reduce the issuance of legally invalid patents. Focuses on fee design, limits on repeat filings, examiner time allocations, and empirical assessment of incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restructure Patent Office fee schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office’s fee schedule should be restructured to minimize the risk that fee revenue will be insufficient to cover operational costs and to diminish the Agency’s financial incentive to grant more patents when revenues fall short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase examination fees to equal examination costs so fees collected at filing cover the costs of examination (PTO estimated ~$4,200 per exam vs current lower fees). Abolish issuance fees (or treat them like renewal fees and decouple from Agency funding) so revenue does not grow only when patents are granted. Keep renewal fees as a mechanism to shorten patent life but decouple renewal income from Agency funding. Rationale: back-ended fees (issuance + renewal) create instability and incentives to grant during shortfalls; empirical evidence (Frakes & Wasserman) shows higher grant rates during budgetary shortfalls. Consider international comparisons (EPO/JPO fees) and small impacts of modest examination fee increases on filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align examination fees with actual examination costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Set examination fees at levels sufficient to meet the true cost of reviewing applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examination fees cover examination costs, the Agency can expand capacity when filings rise and is less likely to act on financial incentives to increase grant rates. Concerns about access for small/micro-entities can be addressed via subsidies or alternative funding; small increases in fees are unlikely to substantially reduce filings because attorney costs dominate. Empirical citation: PTO average examination cost ≈ $4,200 (FY2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate or neutralize issuance fees as a funding source
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove issuance fees (paid only when a patent is granted) or otherwise decouple them from the Agency’s budget to avoid incentivizing grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuance fees are post-allowance and used to bolster examination funding; eliminating or decoupling them reduces the incentive to issue additional patents to raise revenue. If not eliminated, treat issuance fees like renewal fees and route them to a reserve not directly available to increase current operating spending tied to grant rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decouple renewal fee income from Agency funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tie the Patent Office’s operating budget directly to renewal-fee income that depends on patents being in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal fees serve social function (effectively shorten patent life if not paid) but coupling their income to Agency budgets creates perverse incentives. Route renewal revenues to a reserve/subsidy mechanism or otherwise insulate annual operating appropriations from fluctuation in renewal receipts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect small- and micro-entity access when raising fees
rubrics_metrics.description: When increasing examination fees or restructuring fees, preserve reasonable access for small and micro entities through subsidies or maintained discounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include (a) a subsidy paid from renewal fee revenue to small/micro-entities, (b) general revenue subsidies, or (c) maintaining guaranteed discounts but aligning large-entity fees with costs. Tradeoff: shifting subsidy risk to small-entity pool could reduce discounts if that applicant pool grows, so Congress could consider non-fee subsidies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit repeat applications (continuations and RCEs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place meaningful limits on repeat filings so that rejected applicants cannot indefinitely restart the examination process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat filings (continuations and Requests for Continued Examination) constitute a large share of filings (~40% in FY2016) and increase backlog and examination costs. Limits reduce the incentive for the Agency to grant more patents to stem repeat filings. Provide exceptions or safe harbors for legitimate uses (e.g., biotech/pharma refinement) and preserve appeal routes (PTAB and courts) so applicants retain a path to challenge rejections. If USPTO rulemaking authority is insufficient, Congress should delegate explicit authority to limit repeat filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure limits on repeat filings do not unduly harm legitimate applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Design repeat-filing limits to distinguish abusive continuation practice from good-faith further prosecution or necessary refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize industries (e.g., pharmaceuticals, biotech) that file early and legitimately refine claims; allow mechanisms (narrow exceptions, higher fees, or limited continuations) for such cases. Use appeal processes (PTAB, Federal Circuit) as an alternative avenue for applicants who reach repeat-filing limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase time allocations for patent examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate more examination hours per application to allow examiners adequate time to search prior art, compare, and write reasoned rejections when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average examiner time is low (≈19 hours). Empirical evidence shows promotions that cut allocated time are associated with 13–29% higher grant rates, and giving all examiners GS-7-level hours could reduce overall grant rate by roughly 20% (~40,000 fewer patents/year). Increasing hours reduces superficial reviews and likely reduces issuance of invalid patents. Recognize budgetary tradeoffs: more time reduces throughput and costs more in personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust scaling of time reductions upon examiner promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the rate at which allotted examination time is reduced as examiners advance in GS pay grades to avoid providing excessive time pressure on senior examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current promotions reduce allocated hours (roughly 10–15% per GS step), which empirically increases grant rates. Adjust scaling so senior examiners do not face dramatic time cuts that materially raise grant propensity; aim for more homogeneous grant rates across examiners to increase equity and consistency of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical evidence to identify and measure incentives driving grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on rigorous empirical analysis to detect whether Agency features (funding, backlog, time allocations) causally influence grant rates and patent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing grant rates for technologies with historically high renewal or repeat-filing rates vs. others during budget shortfalls; tracking examiner-level grant-rate changes upon promotions; benchmarking US outcomes against EPO/JPO for same applications to assess questionable validity. Use these methods to prioritize reforms and evaluate their impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid funding structures that bias grants toward technologies or applicants that yield higher fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Design fees and funding so the Agency has no financial incentive to preferentially grant patents in technologies with historically high renewal rates or to large entities that pay higher fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back-ended and differential fee benefits create incentives to favor certain technologies (information & communication, health-related) and large-entity applicants. Such bias leads to patentability decisions influenced by finances rather than legal standards. Fee reform and decoupling can mitigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance patent quality improvements against examination capacity and social welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing fee or time-allocation changes, explicitly analyze trade-offs between higher-quality examination (fewer invalid patents) and reduced throughput (longer pendency, higher Agency costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform cost-benefit analyses using empirically estimated parameters (e.g., Frakes & Wasserman estimate doubling examiner time costs ~$660M vs litigation and prosecution savings ~$904M annually). Consider wider societal benefits of reducing invalid patents (reduced troll activity, improved innovation) that may not be fully captured in narrow financial metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure Agency governance provides stable, usable fee revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure mechanisms (fee reserve funds, appropriation practices) allow the Patent Office to access collected fees timely and reduce vulnerability to fee diversion and budgetary shortfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTFRF created by the AIA partially addresses fee diversion by routing excess collections to a reserve, but appropriations and spending caps can still create shortfalls. Stable access to collected fees reduces volatility that can trigger grant-rate responses to budget stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make patentability decisions based solely on legal standards, not budgetary or backlog pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent granting decisions should be determined by statutory patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, utility, written description), not by Agency financial or backlog considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results suggest non-quality factors (funding shortfalls, backlog, examiner time) are currently affecting outcomes. Reforms should aim to align incentives so examiners apply legal standards consistently regardless of Agency budget status.
